Dizzy Gillespie was an American jazz trumpeter, bandleader, and composer whose harmonic innovations, technical virtuosity, and infectiously playful musicianship made him one of bebop's architects.

He was a trumpet virtuoso who pioneered bebop alongside Charlie Parker, introducing rapid bebop lines, complex harmonies, and unprecedented upper-register technique to the trumpet. Gillespie became known for his bent, upturned trumpet bell, a trademark accidental discovery, and his clownish stage persona that contrasted his profound musical sophistication with theatrical humor.

He composed and recorded "A Night in Tunisia" and "Groovin' High," signature bebop standards that showcased his compositional cleverness and improvisational genius. As a bandleader, Gillespie incorporated Afro-Cuban percussion and rhythms into his orchestra, prefiguring jazz's later fusion with world music and establishing himself as a rhythmic innovator.

He performed at the 1945 Bebop at the Philharmonic concerts that introduced bebop to broader audiences, becoming bebop's most public and charismatic face. Gillespie maintained a long career spanning seven decades, continuing to perform and innovate well into the nineteen-nineties. With Charlie Parker, he co-pioneered bebop and recorded many definitive recordings together.
